### Question 1

Enter in the data

60 85 72 59 37 75 93 7 98 63 41 90 5 17 97

Make a stem and leaf plot.

We will call our data "sample1", it is important to use a name which will make sense to use when we come back to this code later on.
```{r}
sample1=c(60,85,72,59,37,75,93,7,98,63,41,90,5,17,97)
```

```{r}
stem(sample1)
```
This default has caused some ambiguity, where is 17 on this output, is 0|7 7 or 17? We can use the option scale to split the output and in this case (scale=2) use twice as many stem options.

```{r}
stem(sample1,scale=2)
```

### Question 3
One can generate random data with the “R" commands. For example
x = rnorm(100)
produces 100 random numbers with a standardised normal distribution. Create two different histograms for two different instances of defining x as above. Do you get the same histograms?

```{r}
norm_samples1=rnorm(100)
norm_samples2=rnorm(100)
```

Lets plot these as a histogram
```{r}
hist(norm_samples1)
hist(norm_samples2)
```
Since the two samples are random they are not the same, although if we have more more data then the two histograms will become more similar.


### Question 4

Data were collected on the time (in days) until each of 200 claims is settled by the
insurer in a certain insurance portfolio. The data are given in the file settle time.txt which
can be found on Canvas under Practical Sheets → Practical Sheet 1.

(a)Download (or copy) the data on your computer and read the values into R.[A useful command in R is settle.times=scan() ].
```{r}
settle.times=scan(file="settle_times.txt")
```

(b)Summarise the data using the mean and the five point summary, and comment
on the symmetry of the distribution of the data based on these measures (useful
commands in R are mean, quantile(), summary() ).

```{r}
cat('The mean of the settle_times data is given by ',mean(settle.times), '\n')
cat('The quantiles of the settle_times data is given by ', quantile(settle.times), '\n')
print('The summary of the settle_times data is given by')
summary(settle.times)
```
The mean is considerably larger than the median, implying that the distribution is skewed to the right. Also, the maximum value is far away from the median and the third quartile, which reveals a long right tail.

(c) Produce a frequency table of the times to settlement. It may be useful to divide the range of
the data into intervals of 30 days, i.e. [0, 30), [30, 60), . . . . [390, 420). Note that whether an
interval is right-open or left-open will make a difference. In R you can do this as follows:

```{r}
settle.breaks = seq(0,420,by=30)
settle.table = table(cut(settle.times, breaks = settle.breaks,
right=F))
settle.table
```

(d) Draw a histogram of the data (using the same intervals as in the table above) and a boxplot.

```{r}
hist(settle.times,breaks=settle.breaks,freq=TRUE,col="gray",
main="Histogram of claims settling time",xlab="Days")
boxplot(settle.times, horizontal = T)
```

(e) Comment briefly on the shape of the distribution of the data. Can you suggest a suitable
theoretical distribution for the time until claims are settled in this portfolio?

It is obvious that the distribution of time to settlement for these claims is positively skewed, with a mode close to zero. An exponential model may be appropriate.

### Question 5

The following data are a sample from a survey on property prices (in £1000) in a city in Scotland:

191.6 216.7 196.6 220.7 301.0 236.1 142.4 190.4 200.9 241.8
184.9 202.1 156.7 198.1 240.1 169.7 151.8 257.0 347.9 281.6

These data have been considered in Tutorial 1 Question 8.
In addition to the data above, suppose that a similar survey in a different Scottish city gave the
following property prices (again in £1000):

130.4 155.1 155.7 187.2 100.4 142.8 118.3 154.8 121.1 126.1
137.8 158.7 147.0 132.3 133.0 127.0 88.6 98.8 155.4 124.9

(a) Compare the dispersion of the two data sets using histograms (remember to put the two data
sets on the same scale for comparison).

First we add the data
```{r}
property1 = c(191.6,216.7,196.6,220.7,301.0,236.1,142.4,190.4,200.9,241.8,184.9,202.1,156.7,198.1,240.1,169.7,151.8,257.0,347.9,281.6)
property2 = c(130.4,155.1, 155.7, 187.2, 100.4, 142.8, 118.3, 154.8, 121.1, 126.1, 137.8, 158.7, 147.0, 132.3, 133.0, 127.0, 88.6, 98.8, 155.4, 124.9)
```

Next we draw the two histograms using the option xlim to ensure the scales are the same
```{r}
hist(property1,xlim=c(80,350))
hist(property2,xlim=c(80,350))
```

(b) Compare the dispersion of the two data sets using boxplots again putting the two data sets
on the same scale for comparison.

```{r}
boxplot(property1,property2)
```

(c) Now compare the dispersion of the two samples using appropriate numerical measures of
spread. (Hint: is the variance suitable here?)

We start by calculating the variances.
```{r}
print(paste0("Variance of City 1: ", var(property1)))
print(paste0("Variance of City 2: ", var(property2)))
```
Comment: The property price of City 1 has greater dispersion than of City 2, since it has larger variance
as can be seen above and also higher interquartile range of about 50,000 pounds compared with City 2
of approximately 30,000 pounds.
Notice (e.g. from the boxplot above) that the level of prices is different in the two cities. Remember that
the variance depends on the scale of the measured values, so it may not be appropriate for comparisons
here. Instead, calculate the coefficient of variation, which doesn't depend on the scale of the data:

```{r}
print(paste0("Coefficient of variation of City 1: ", sd(property1)/mean(property1)))
print(paste0("Coefficient of variation of City 1: ", sd(property2)/mean(property2)))
```
The coefficient of variation for the two data sets is closer than the standard deviation, implying that the variation of the prices in the two cities is not as different as the sample variances suggest.

### Question 6

Produce functions in R to calculate the coefficient of symmetry and the kurtosis using the code
below.
```{r}
beta1.fn = function(x)
{
  sum.dev3 = sum( (x - mean(x))^3 )
  b1 = (sum.dev3/length(x))/(sd(x))^3
  cat("\n","Coefficient of symmetry for these data is: ",
  b1, "\n\n")
}

kurtosis.fn = function(x)
{
  sum.dev4 = sum( (x - mean(x))^4 )
  k1 = ((sum.dev4/length(x))/(sd(x))^4)-3
  cat("\n","Kurtosis for these data is: ", k1, "\n\n")
}
```

Find the mean, standard deviation, coefficient of symmetry and kurtosis for the following data:
```{r}
data6=c(33, 23, 34, 27, 32, 45, 5, 50, 27, 25, 25, 8, 27, 13, 31, 9, 16, 10, 40, 35, 41, 4, 22, 41, 43, 52, 25, 40, 27, 22)
```
Using these new functions we have
```{r}
cat("\n","Mean for this data is : ", mean(data6), "\n\n")
cat("\n","Standard Deviation for this data is : ", sd(data6), "\n\n")
beta1.fn(data6)
kurtosis.fn(data6)
```

### Question 10

A coin is given 10 independent tosses, each of which lands heads with probability p. Let the random
variable N denote the total number of heads obtained. Then, in R, given p and any value of n, we
can calculate the probability of n heads as
dbinom(n,10,p)

Set p = 0.3 (not a very fair coin!) and find the probabilities of various values of n in the range 0 to
10.
```{r}
for (n in 0:10) {
 print(paste0(" For n=",n," the probability of n heads is ",dbinom(n,10,0.3)))
}

```
Now generate the entire probability function of the random variable N with
```{r}
pf = dbinom(0:10,10,0.3)
```
Use sum to verify that the sum of these probabilities is 1, and plot a bar chart to show their
distribution with
barplot(pf, names = 0:10)

To verify the probabilities sum to one:
```{r}
sum(pf)
```
Which gives 1 as we expect.

For the bar plot:
```{r}
barplot(pf,names.arg=0:10)
```
What are the first, second, and third most likely numbers of heads? 

The most likely numbers of heads are 3,2 then 4.

Calculate the mean and standard deviation of this distribution with
```{r}
mn = sum(0:10 * pf)
cat("\n","The expected value is ",mn,"\n")
stdev = sqrt(sum((0:10)^2 * pf) - mn^2)
cat("\n","The standard deviation is ",stdev,"\n")
```

Verify that the values obtained agree with those obtained from your own knowledge of the binomial
distribution.

Comment: The value obtained agrees because this is a Normal approximation to the Binomial distribution. 
$$\text{Mean} = n*p = 10*0.3 = 3$$
$$\text{Standard deviation} = \sqrt{n*p*(1-p)} = \sqrt{10*0.3*0.7} = 1.449138$$
